subtitle: The interactive process is, at heart, a respectful and focused conversation. Use it to understand a barrier at work, compare adjustments that could be effective and then follow through.
scope: For DHS supervisors and managers participating in employment accommodation conversations with the employee and the agency ADA Coordinator. Use verified agency procedures and decision authority. The course’s practice dialogue supports learning; it does not make a medical, eligibility, hardship or personnel decision.
introTranscript: The interactive process is a shared exchange about a disability-related work barrier and an effective accommodation. It is not a debate about whether a person deserves help or a supervisor’s medical interview. A good conversation separates what is already known, what needs clarification and who is responsible for the next step. This course follows a practice analyst whose work tool and meeting arrangements create barriers. You will practice opening the conversation, clarifying duties, protecting documentation, comparing options, communicating a decision and checking whether it works. Listen with curiosity, explain the work accurately and keep formal decisions with the responsible agency process.

lessons.title: Open the conversation with a clear purpose
lessons.summary: A useful opening explains the task, roles and next step without asking the person to defend their disability.
lessons.objective: Explain the purpose of an interactive accommodation conversation in plain language.
objectives: Explain the purpose of an interactive accommodation conversation in plain language.
Invite a work-focused account of the barrier without requesting medical documentation.
Recognize the person’s option to request a support person under the state process.
takeaways: The conversation concerns the work barrier and effective adjustment, not whether someone deserves help.
Explain the roles and use an accessible way to meet or communicate.
A support person can assist the requester; clarify participation without assuming incapacity.
lessons.statement: A clear opening makes it easier for the person and the agency to exchange the information needed for a sound next step.

image.caption: A shared conversation can be respectful and practical without becoming a medical interview.

intro.heading: Set the purpose before asking questions
intro.body:
A practice analyst asks for a disability-related change in a reporting tool and a recurring meeting arrangement. Their supervisor arranges a conversation with the appropriate accommodation staff. A useful opening explains that the purpose is to understand the work barrier and consider effective options through the agency process. It identifies the participants’ roles and avoids promising an outcome before the necessary review.

MMB Policy 1433 describes an exchange when the need or effective adjustment is not clear, options conflict or circumstances change. The employee can request a support person to participate, including an identified individual, union representative or other support described in the process. A support person may help with questions, notes or emotional support. Their presence does not mean the employee lacks decision-making ability or no longer speaks for themselves. Clarify the employee’s preferred participation and protect confidentiality.

The meeting itself should be usable. Ask about the format, timing and communication support needed for this conversation without requiring a diagnosis. Provide an agenda that explains the work questions. A fast, dense meeting with unexplained roles can reproduce the barrier the process is meant to address. If a different exchange is more effective, use the appropriate agency process to arrange it.

A supervisor can say, “Let’s look at the task you need to complete, the barrier and the options to consider. The coordinator will guide the formal questions, and we will be clear about what happens next.” This is a suggested learning example, not a required script. The important features are purpose, respect and a real next step. The process should not become a test of the person’s legal vocabulary or willingness to share private medical details.

inThisLesson: Invite the person’s account of the work barrier.
lessons.keyStatement: Begin with a shared purpose and an understandable process, not a demand for personal proof.

flashcards.back: A shared exchange to understand the relevant work barrier and identify an effective accommodation, through the responsible employment process.
Someone the requester identifies to assist their participation, such as with notes, questions or support. The requester’s voice and choices remain central.
Knowing who contributes work information, who handles documentation and who makes the formal decision.
An exchange arranged so the person can understand, participate and respond effectively, including appropriate format or support.

items.title: Explain the purpose
items.body: Name the work barrier and which options this exchange can consider. A clear purpose helps the employee contribute relevant task experience without feeling that the meeting is a test of credibility. It also helps other participants separate an exploratory discussion from a final decision. Preserve appropriate documentation and formal questions in their assigned roles rather than asking the employee to present a medical case to everyone.

items.title: Clarify who is there
items.body: Identify the supervisor, coordinator and any support person requested under the policy, explaining their roles and confidentiality expectations. A support person may help with notes or questions without replacing the employee’s voice or making every decision. Rejecting such participation merely because the employee should manage alone is not the policy approach. Keep the purpose of each participant clear so helpful support does not become unnecessary disclosure.

items.title: Ask about participation
items.body: Provide a useful agenda and ask about the format or communication support needed for participation. An accommodation discussion itself needs to be usable. Do not require the employee to describe a diagnosis to everyone before clarifying how the exchange will work. Coordinate uncertain arrangements with the responsible process so an invitation to discuss the barrier does not create a new one.

tabs.label: Welcoming and specific
tabs.body: A welcoming opening names a specific purpose: understand the work barrier and consider effective options through the accommodation process. This gives the employee a way to contribute relevant experience without making the meeting a credibility test. Explain who is present and the next step. For example, a requested support person can help clarify questions while the employee’s own voice remains central; welcoming language does not pre-decide the result.

tabs.label: Too adversarial
tabs.body: An adversarial opening asks the employee to prove that they deserve a different arrangement before the task is understood. It can discourage the information an interactive process needs and blur work discussion with medical inquiry. Replace that challenge with the relevant task, barrier and options, while leaving appropriate documentation to the ADA Coordinator. The aim is a supported decision, not a judgment made from how convincingly someone presents a personal story.

tabs.label: Too vague
tabs.body: A vague opening offers no purpose, role or next step. The employee may not know whether an option is being discussed, approved or ignored, and a supervisor may assume that another office will act. State what this conversation can examine and who is responsible for unresolved questions. Clear coordination makes participation useful without promising an outcome or implying that every participant has the same decision authority.

check.question: An employee asks to bring a support person to an accommodation conversation. What is the sound response?
check.correct: Follow the state and agency process, clarify the person’s role and support the employee’s own participation and confidentiality.
wrong: Assume the support person will make every decision for the employee.
Reject the idea because employees must manage all conversations alone.
Require the support person to explain the employee’s diagnosis to the team.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. Support-person participation is part of the policy’s process. Clarify the contribution without taking away the employee’s voice or disclosing unnecessary medical details.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A requested support person is allowed within the policy process and should not be rejected merely because the employee is expected to manage alone. Their presence does not establish incapacity or give them every decision. Requiring a medical presentation to the team would also create unnecessary disclosure. Clarify the contribution, protect confidentiality and support the employee’s own participation.

items.text: We will discuss the task, the barrier and possible effective adjustments.
Explain your complete medical history before you can ask questions.
The coordinator handles formal documentation questions; the supervisor describes the work.
Which format would help you take part in this conversation?
We will decide about you while you wait outside without an explanation.
Your support person can help you participate; your own choices remain central.

lessons.next: The next lesson builds a shared description of the task so the discussion has a concrete purpose.

scenario.context: A practice analyst requests an accessible format for the conversation and asks to bring a support person. A supervisor worries that these requests will make the discussion less efficient.
options: Use the agency process to arrange effective participation and clarify roles before discussing the work.
Ignore the requests and hold the meeting in the usual format.
Treat the support request as evidence the analyst cannot perform the job.
responses: This supports a useful exchange while preserving the employee’s role and confidentiality. Efficiency should include whether people can participate meaningfully.
The usual format may reproduce the barrier. An inaccessible exchange can prevent the information needed for an effective decision.
This makes an unsupported ability inference from the person’s participation needs.

lessons.transfer: Write a short opening for the practice conversation: purpose, participant roles and an invitation to explain the work barrier. Do not request a diagnosis.

move.control: You can make the conversation understandable and support participation.
move.failure: The person is expected to defend themselves before the work is discussed.
move.next: Use a clear agenda and confirm the appropriate participants and communication arrangements.

lessons.title: Build a shared picture of the task
lessons.summary: Clarify the duty, the barrier and the result before considering a solution.
lessons.objective: Describe a fundamental job duty separately from a customary method.
objectives: Describe a fundamental job duty separately from a customary method.
Summarize the person’s account of a barrier without adding a diagnosis assumption.
Identify an uncertainty that needs work evidence or specialist guidance.
takeaways: A shared task description prevents options from being compared against different goals.
Check your understanding with the person rather than substituting your own explanation.
Distinguish facts, assumptions and questions that need further review.
lessons.statement: The most useful solution discussion starts with agreement about what the task needs to accomplish and where the barrier occurs.

image.caption: A task can be examined step by step while the person retains their own account of the difficulty.

intro.heading: Describe the result before the method
intro.body:
In the practice analyst’s task, the essential result is to review service data accurately and prepare an understandable report. The current method requires repeated mouse use and a dense table view. The supervisor initially describes mouse use as an essential function because everyone currently works that way. This needs reconsideration. A fundamental duty is not automatically the same as the traditional tool or movement used to carry it out. The actual position and work evidence matter.

Ask the person where the task becomes difficult and what an adjustment needs to allow. A useful summary might be, “You need to compare the listed amounts accurately, and the current way of moving between fields is the barrier you want addressed. Have I understood that?” This checks the work account without asking the supervisor to assess the medical condition. The coordinator handles appropriate documentation and eligibility questions.

The supervisor can contribute deadlines, quality requirements and operating conditions. Be specific about what is genuinely fixed and what is a habit that could change. If a claimed requirement is uncertain, identify it for review rather than defending it as obvious. Consider the person’s experience and specialist advice about the tool; neither should be replaced by a guess based on appearance or diagnosis.

Record a short shared work description through the authorized process. It should distinguish known facts, the desired result and open questions. This is not a medical dossier or a team-wide explanation of the employee’s private information. The purpose is to make the option comparison meaningful. If two people are describing different tasks, pause to clarify before discussing cost or choosing an adjustment.

inThisLesson: Separate a method from a duty.
Check the person’s account of the barrier.
lessons.keyStatement: A shared task description makes the next decision clearer; a diagnosis assumption makes it less reliable.

flashcards.back: An essential job function assessed from relevant evidence about the position and actual work.
The way the task is usually performed. It may be changed without removing the essential result.
A clear account of the task, barrier, needed result and unanswered questions that participants understand in the same way.
A brief restatement of what you heard, offered for correction rather than presented as the final interpretation.

accordion.heading: Four parts of the task description

items.title: The required result
items.body: Explain the output and relevant quality requirements, using the actual position and work. Accurate field review describes a result more clearly than insisting on a traditional input device. This gives the process a basis for examining alternatives while retaining essential duties. Seek guidance where that distinction is uncertain rather than changing the job description privately to reach a preferred outcome.

items.title: The reported barrier
items.body: Let the employee explain where the task becomes difficult and check the accuracy of your task-focused summary. For example, the problem may concern reaching particular fields rather than reading the entire report. That distinction affects which options need consideration. Do not translate the description into a diagnosis or assume that one employee’s experience establishes every person’s needs.

items.title: The conditions
items.body: Identify the relevant tools, timing and environments. An option that works in a demonstration may interact differently with the configured system used for the actual task. Conditions may call for specialist input through the responsible process. Describe these facts precisely rather than using a broad product preference as proof that an alternative is effective or impossible.

items.title: The unknowns
items.body: Name what still requires evidence or guidance and the responsible next step. If effectiveness is untested, say so rather than filling the gap with a stereotype about the condition. Uncertainty does not mean the employee lacks credibility or that the requested option must be approved automatically. It gives the interactive process a clearer question to examine.

tabs.label: Duty
tabs.body: A duty description identifies what the job needs to accomplish, such as accurate review of required fields. Verify the description against the position and actual work rather than choosing wording to favor a tool. This lets the process ask whether another method preserves the essential result. A careful description does not mean the supervisor can privately remove an essential duty or determine every accommodation question.

tabs.label: Method
tabs.body: Mouse use describes one way of moving through fields, not automatically the required job result. If another input method supports accurate review, it may be relevant to the comparison. Consider the actual task and seek guidance on essential-function questions rather than treating widespread use as sufficient evidence. Equally, a proposed alternative must be examined for effectiveness; being different or preferred does not by itself establish the result.

tabs.label: Assumption
tabs.body: A diagnosis-based prediction about whether someone can review data substitutes a group assumption for work and accommodation evidence. Describe the task and examine the actual barrier through the appropriate process. This leaves room for an effective adjustment and a case-specific decision without asking the supervisor to diagnose the employee. The person’s account is important, but neither identity nor a tool preference alone decides every job requirement.

check.question: Which description most clearly separates a duty from a method?
check.correct: The task requires accurate field review; mouse use is the current method whose alternatives should be examined.
wrong: Mouse use is essential simply because everyone uses it now.
A diagnosis tells us whether the person can review a report.
The employee’s preferred tool automatically changes every job requirement.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. This identifies the required result and leaves room to examine an effective method through the proper process.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Reconsider the actual work. Tradition, a diagnosis or a tool preference alone does not define the essential function or the formal decision.

items.text: The report must accurately reconcile the stated amounts.
The current tool is normally operated with a mouse.
This condition means the person cannot analyze data.
The report is due on the date specified in the project plan.
Meetings currently use one particular display arrangement.
A different method must be unfair to other staff.

lessons.next: The next lesson addresses what information is genuinely needed and who may request it.

scenario.context: In this example, a supervisor and employee agree that accurate report review is required but disagree about whether the current mouse-based method is essential.
scenario.prompt: What is the best next step?
options: Assume the method is essential because it is familiar.
Review the actual duty and operating evidence with the responsible staff, while considering whether another effective method preserves the result.
Remove every report duty before considering an adjustment.
responses: Familiarity is not evidence that a method is fundamental. The relevant duty and alternatives need examination.
This keeps the work requirement clear while examining the method through the appropriate process.
Accommodation does not automatically remove essential duties. The process considers effective adjustments and the applicable boundaries.

lessons.transfer: For a practice task, write one required result, one current method and one open question. Add a summary you could offer the person for correction.

move.control: You can describe the actual work and check your understanding.
move.failure: A familiar practice is defended as essential without evidence.
move.next: Clarify the task before comparing options or raising formal limits.

lessons.title: Ask only for information the process needs
lessons.summary: Appropriate documentation answers a relevant question; it is not a general search through a person’s medical history.
lessons.objective: Distinguish a supervisor’s work discussion from the coordinator’s documentation role.
objectives: Distinguish a supervisor’s work discussion from the coordinator’s documentation role.
Explain why broad medical records are not an appropriate accommodation request under the state policy.
Choose a confidential response when medical information is volunteered or misdirected.
takeaways: The ADA Coordinator determines and requests appropriate accommodation documentation.
Supervisors and managers do not request medical information or documentation in this process.
Confidentiality applies to medical information and accommodation status.
lessons.statement: Relevant information supports the decision. Unnecessary personal information creates risk without making the work discussion better.

image.caption: A clear boundary around personal information protects the person and improves the focus of the conversation.

intro.heading: Keep documentation relevant and properly handled
intro.body:
Sometimes the disability-related need is apparent or already known; sometimes the authorized process needs information to understand whether a covered disability and accommodation need exist. MMB Policy 1433 assigns these questions to the agency ADA Coordinator. Supervisors and managers must not request medical information or documentation from the applicant or employee seeking accommodation. Their contribution remains the work duties, conditions and implementation facts.

The policy says appropriate documentation is specifically related to the accommodation request and ability to perform essential functions. It also says agencies must not request medical records, which are not appropriate documentation and cannot be accepted in this process. A complete medical file can contain unrelated information and is not a useful shortcut to a sound decision. The coordinator uses the policy’s documentation procedure and necessary authorization for communication with a medical provider. The employee has responsibilities within that procedure, but a supervisor should not invent a parallel collection route.

If an employee sends medical information to the supervisor without being asked, treat it as confidential. Seek the appropriate directions for handling and routing it. Do not attach it to team meeting notes, a shared performance folder or a learning reflection. Medical information collected in the accommodation process is separately maintained with access limited as the policy describes. People implementing an adjustment may receive necessary work restrictions and arrangements; that is not unrestricted permission to share the diagnosis.

When a documentation question slows the process, ask the coordinator to explain what is needed and the next step to the requester. Do not describe every request as unsubstantiated until medical proof arrives. The appropriate process decides the relevant need while keeping the conversation focused and respectful.

inThisLesson: Distinguish relevant documentation from broad records.
Keep learning notes separate from personnel records.
lessons.keyStatement: A supervisor does not need a medical file to contribute an accurate account of the work.

flashcards.back: Appropriate information connected to disability and the accommodation need, requested through the coordinator’s process when needed.
A broader medical history or file. The state accommodation policy says these records are not appropriate documentation and cannot be accepted.
Permission used in the policy’s process before the coordinator communicates with a medical provider. The supervisor does not create a separate provider inquiry.
Collecting, maintaining and sharing protected information only through the authorized process and its limited purposes.

items.title: Is more information needed?
items.body: The coordinator considers whether the disability or accommodation need is already evident or sufficiently known. Appropriate documentation may be necessary in some cases, but additional medical material is not a universal opening requirement. This avoids making every employee produce a broad history before the task can be discussed. The supervisor contributes work facts without deciding or soliciting the medical evidence.

items.title: Who requests it?
items.body: The agency ADA Coordinator makes appropriate medical-documentation requests under Policy 1433. Supervisors and managers must not solicit that information, even with a promise of privacy or a wish to accelerate the review. A supervisor can explain the task and route a documentation question. Agencies also must not request or accept medical records; the proper process seeks the relevant information the policy permits.

items.title: Who receives implementation details?
items.body: People with an authorized need may receive the work restrictions and arrangements required for implementation within the policy limits. Curiosity or general team involvement does not establish that need. For example, a coworker may need handoff timing without confirmation of accommodation status. Keep medical and confidential accommodation information in the proper process rather than using broad disclosure to win agreement for a work change.

tabs.label: Work description
tabs.body: The supervisor contributes work facts: the required fields, environment, timing and reported task barrier. These can help the process compare options without diagnosis or treatment details. Ask whether your summary accurately describes the task, not for a medical history. This keeps useful job knowledge available while preserving Policy 1433’s rule that supervisors and managers must not request accommodation medical information or documentation.

tabs.label: Documentation process
tabs.body: The agency ADA Coordinator handles appropriate, relevant documentation requests under the policy, including required authorization for provider communication. Documentation is not automatically needed when the disability and need are already evident or sufficiently known. A complete medical file is not an appropriate shortcut. Let the coordinator determine the need and proper scope rather than making paperwork collection a supervisor’s test of whether the request deserves attention.

tabs.label: Learning reflection
tabs.body: Course reflection uses practice or appropriately non-identifying material. The accommodation process’s authority to hold necessary confidential information does not make that information suitable for a learning answer. A useful example can state that a table-review barrier remained without copying an employee’s medical file or request record. Preserve the original formal records in their responsible process and examine the learning question without unnecessary personal detail.

check.question: A supervisor wants to request the employee’s entire medical file to speed the accommodation review. What should happen?
check.correct: The supervisor should not request medical information; the ADA Coordinator determines appropriate, relevant documentation through the policy process.
wrong: Request the file and put it in the shared project folder.
Ask coworkers to interpret the medical file.
Treat a complete file as mandatory for every request.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The policy assigns documentation requests to the coordinator and excludes broad medical records as appropriate documentation. Work information can be contributed without collecting a medical history.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A supervisor must not request accommodation medical information or documentation. A shared project folder would spread confidential material, and coworkers are not the appropriate people to interpret a medical file. A complete file is not mandatory for every request and agencies must not request or accept medical records. Let the ADA Coordinator determine appropriate relevant documentation under the policy while contributing the work facts the process needs.

sorting.heading: Keep the information in its proper role

items.text: The report requires comparing six specified fields.
Is appropriate disability-related documentation needed in this case?
A medical attachment is copied into the whole team’s notes.
The current task uses two tools and a weekly review meeting.
What authorization is required before contacting a provider?
The employee’s diagnosis is used as a label in the public work calendar.

lessons.next: The next lesson compares options against the shared work purpose instead of treating a familiar option as automatically effective.

scenario.context: In this example, an employee voluntarily emails medical information to a supervisor during the discussion. The supervisor is unsure what to do with it.
options: Forward it to every colleague so they understand the request.
Ignore confidentiality because the employee volunteered it.
Treat it as confidential, seek the proper handling directions and keep the work discussion focused on the task.
responses: Broad forwarding exposes private information and does not help the appropriate review.
Volunteered medical information remains confidential; the manner of disclosure does not erase the handling obligations.
This protects the information and seeks the responsible process rather than creating an informal medical record.

lessons.transfer: Identify a practice work fact the supervisor can provide and a documentation question for the coordinator. Keep all personal medical details out of the exercise.

move.control: You can contribute useful work facts and preserve confidentiality.
move.failure: A desire for certainty turns into collecting an unnecessary medical history.
move.next: Use the coordinator’s route for documentation and verify how your role should handle any information received.

lessons.title: Compare options by whether they work
lessons.summary: Consider the person’s preference and the actual task, with formal limits handled through the authorized process.
lessons.objective: Compare two options against a specific work result and barrier.
objectives: Compare two options against a specific work result and barrier.
Explain the difference between an effective alternative and a merely available alternative.
Identify a formal hardship or threat question that requires the responsible decision process.
takeaways: Effectiveness is the central question; availability alone is not enough.
The person’s preference receives serious consideration, while another effective option may be offered.
The supervisor contributes work evidence rather than deciding from stereotypes or local budget assumptions.
lessons.statement: An option is useful when it addresses the barrier in the real task, not merely when it is easy for the team to provide.

image.caption: A shared comparison can reveal why a proposed adjustment works or leaves a barrier unresolved.

intro.heading: Make the comparison concrete
intro.body:
The practice analyst prefers a particular tool. The agency already has another tool that appears similar. A respectful exchange examines what each option permits in the actual task. Can the analyst reach every field, compare the required information and produce the report accurately? Are the relevant work conditions the same as in the demonstration? The employee’s account of the barrier and specialist knowledge of the tool both help answer these questions.

Under MMB Policy 1433, the employee’s preference is seriously considered, but the agency may provide another effective accommodation. That is a meaningful boundary: an alternative must be effective for the relevant need. An option is not adequate simply because it is cheaper, familiar or liked by coworkers. Nor does the preferred option automatically settle every formal question. The decision belongs to the authorized process, with the employee’s participation and the relevant evidence.

Where an option’s effectiveness is uncertain, identify what needs checking rather than declaring success. A practical comparison or trial may help when arranged through the appropriate process. Explain the purpose, what will be examined, who will respond and how the person can report an unresolved barrier. Do not use an endless trial to delay a necessary decision or leave the person without effective support.

Formal limits need proper assessment. Undue hardship depends on case-specific resource and operational factors, not the supervisor’s inconvenience alone. Direct threat depends on individualized objective evidence about significant risk, not a diagnosis stereotype. Consult the ADA Coordinator as required, especially before denial. A careful comparison can support the decision without pretending the supervisor’s worksheet establishes legal eligibility or an exception.

inThisLesson: Use the work result as the comparison point.
Route formal limits to the responsible process.
lessons.keyStatement: The question is not whether an alternative exists; it is whether an effective alternative exists for this need.

flashcards.back: Another adjustment that addresses the relevant barrier and provides the employment opportunity the accommodation is intended to support.
The person’s desired adjustment, which the state policy says should be seriously considered.
An examination of options against the actual duty, barrier, conditions and required result.
A question such as undue hardship or direct threat that must be evaluated case by case through the proper authority and consultation.

items.title: What must it accomplish?
items.body: Use the shared task description to state what an option must accomplish. If accurate field review is the purpose, compare access to the required fields under relevant conditions. Tool appearance or a feature list can inform a question without proving that result. An explained purpose makes a trial or specialist check meaningful and prevents the comparison from becoming a contest between product preferences.

items.title: What does the person report?
items.body: Listen to the employee’s account of why an option helps or fails, and seriously consider their preference through the process. A reported barrier can point to a task condition that the demonstration missed. Seek appropriate specialist input where needed rather than replacing the account with coworker convenience. This informs an effectiveness comparison without guaranteeing that every preferred option must be selected.

items.title: What remains uncertain?
items.body: Identify the remaining check and who will complete it. A workaround that has been proposed but not used may still be unverified for the task. Record the uncertainty through the proper process and follow up; do not make the employee’s lack of complaint prove success. The comparison should distinguish an available idea from evidence that it removes the actual barrier.

items.title: Who decides?
items.body: Keep the formal decision with verified agency authority and involve the coordinator for medical, hardship, direct-threat or denial questions. A supervisor’s knowledge of the work is valuable but not unlimited decision authority. Check actual delegation and required consultation. This permits useful collaboration without turning a task conversation into an informal denial based only on local budget or coworker preference.

tabs.label: Supported
tabs.body: A statement that the configured option allowed required fields to be reviewed under checked conditions is relevant task evidence. Describe those conditions and any limits so the decision maker can evaluate what the check establishes. It is stronger than a product slogan, but should not become a claim that every future task or version will work. Effectiveness for the employee and purpose remains the important comparison.

tabs.label: Not yet established
tabs.body: An already-owned product may be available quickly, but ownership does not show that it removes this barrier. Ask what actual-task check remains and who can contribute appropriate evidence. The employee’s reported difficulty should inform the comparison rather than be dismissed because purchasing was previously completed. Availability and resources matter in the proper process; they do not replace the effectiveness question.

tabs.label: Unsupported
tabs.body: A popular tool can still fail for the employee’s required task. Coworker preference describes the team’s experience, not the employee’s access or a final accommodation decision. Likewise, a polished demonstration may omit the very field-review step that creates the barrier. Return to the shared task, employee input and appropriate assessment rather than treating convenience or appearance as proof.

check.question: Which statement best supports an alternative accommodation?
check.correct: The alternative addresses the relevant barrier in the actual work task, with its effectiveness considered through the process.
wrong: The alternative is already owned, so no further question matters.
Coworkers consider the employee’s preference inconvenient.
The alternative has a polished demonstration but the required task remains untested.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. A relevant effectiveness comparison supports the decision. Availability, preference and appearance do not by themselves establish that the person can perform the needed task.
check.feedbackIncorrect: Ownership shows availability, not effectiveness for the actual barrier. Coworker inconvenience does not replace the employee’s need or serious consideration of their preference. A polished demonstration may not test the required task at all. Compare the actual purpose, conditions and evidence through the accommodation process before treating an alternative as effective.

items.text: The option permits accurate review of all required fields in the actual setup.
Will the tool still work with the report template the unit uses?
It is cheap, so it is automatically an effective accommodation.
The employee explains a tested way the option removes the reported barrier.
Who will verify the recurring meeting arrangement?
A condition’s name tells us which tool every person needs.

lessons.next: The next lesson looks at communicating a decision clearly, including when a requested option is not the one offered.

scenario.context: In this example, an employee says the available tool still cannot reach two essential report fields. A supervisor wants to declare the alternative effective because it worked in a general demonstration.
options: Examine the actual fields and barrier with the employee and appropriate staff before deciding the alternative is effective.
Require the employee to accept it because a demonstration succeeded.
Stop considering every possible adjustment because one option failed.
responses: This addresses the relevant uncertainty. A general demonstration is not a substitute for task evidence in the actual setup.
The known barrier remains. Acceptance cannot be assumed from success in a different task.
One failed option does not establish that no effective accommodation exists. Continue through the authorized process.

lessons.transfer: Compare two practice options using the same four questions: required result, addressed barrier, remaining uncertainty and responsible decision maker.

move.control: You can make the comparison specific and contribute relevant work evidence.
move.failure: Availability or price is used as a substitute for effectiveness.
move.next: Confirm how the proposed option works in the actual task and route formal limits through the coordinator.

lessons.title: Explain the decision and the next step
lessons.summary: A clear decision distinguishes what is approved, what is pending and why another option or denial is being communicated.
lessons.objective: Distinguish an option discussion from an authorized final decision.
objectives: Distinguish an option discussion from an authorized final decision.
Identify the state policy’s requirements for written denial explanations and review information.
Draft a plain-language implementation update without exposing medical details.
takeaways: Know who has authority to communicate the formal decision.
The coordinator must be consulted before denial; the policy requires a plain-language written explanation.
A different offered option needs an explanation of why it is effective, not merely why it costs less.
lessons.statement: The person should understand the decision, its reasons and their next options without having to interpret vague institutional language.

image.caption: Clear communication turns a decision into an understandable next step.

intro.heading: Say what has been decided and what remains
intro.body:
An accommodation conversation can produce several possibilities before the authorized decision maker chooses a course of action. A supervisor should not treat an informal suggestion as final approval or denial. Verify the agency authority and use the appropriate process to communicate the result. The employee should know what is approved, what remains under consideration and what will happen next.

MMB Policy 1433 requires contact with the agency ADA Coordinator for assistance and guidance before denial of any request. Denial reasons must be provided in writing, using plain language and specific explanations. If the agency denies a requested option but offers another accommodation, the communication explains both why the requested option is denied and why the alternative will be effective. Saying only “not feasible” or “policy does not allow it” leaves the person without a useful explanation and may conceal an unsupported assumption.

Agencies must also designate a process for review when a requester appeals a denial. The policy describes agency review and notice of the statutory right to file a charge with the appropriate enforcement agencies. A supervisor should use the verified agency process and formal notices, not invent an appeal route or discourage the person from using it. Do not create a grievance or legal deadline from this course’s practice discussion.

For an approved adjustment, the next step is implementation. State the responsible contact and what the person can expect, including any pending equipment or coordination. Keep medical and accommodation information confidential in work coordination. If something remains unresolved, say so. Respectful communication is compatible with a difficult decision: it explains the relevant reasons, recognizes the person’s questions and keeps the correct review options available.

inThisLesson: Read the required features of a denial explanation.
Name the implementation or review next step.
lessons.keyStatement: A clear explanation is part of the process, especially when the person did not receive the option they requested.

flashcards.back: An approval or denial made through the agency’s assigned authority and required consultation, rather than an informal supervisor conclusion.
A specific, understandable explanation of the decision and its relevant facts, without unexplained shorthand.
The agency’s established route for a person to seek review of a denial. Use current official information rather than inventing a procedure.
The practical actions, responsible contacts and pending steps needed to make an approved adjustment available.

items.title: The result
items.body: Check whether the message clearly distinguishes approval, denial, a pending question and a proposed alternative. These are different states with different responsibilities. An option suggested during discussion should not be described as accepted or implemented without that basis. Accurate wording helps the employee understand what can be followed up and prevents participants from assuming that another person has already completed the next step.

items.title: The explanation
items.body: A denial needs specific written reasons in plain language following the required coordinator consultation. When a different option is offered, explain why the requested one was denied and why the offered one will be effective. Price alone does not supply that comparison. A reasoned explanation supports an understandable response and review through the designated process rather than an unexamined claim that the supervisor has decided.

items.title: The next route
items.body: Use current formal review information and confirmed implementation contacts. Do not invent an appeal route, tell the employee there can be no review or promise an unsupported delivery date. The person needs to know both how a decision may be reviewed and who will arrange an approved change. These distinct next steps keep an understandable letter connected to actual follow-through.

tabs.label: Discussion note
tabs.body: A discussion note records options and unanswered questions through the proper process. It can help people prepare the next step, but a suggested alternative is not automatically approved, accepted or implemented. Label the current state accurately in ordinary language. Otherwise an employee may think the request is decided while a supervisor thinks another office is still reviewing it, leaving a useful conversation without clear responsibility.

tabs.label: Formal decision
tabs.body: A formal decision communicates the authorized result, with the required explanation and review information under current agency procedures. Policy 1433 requires coordinator consultation before denial and specific written reasons. If another option is offered instead, explain why the requested option was denied and why the offered one will be effective. This gives the person something understandable to respond to rather than a generic budget or reasonableness label.

tabs.label: Work coordination
tabs.body: Work coordination explains what colleagues need to do, such as covering an assignment or following an approved schedule. It does not need to announce disability or accommodation status. A team can receive a clear operational message while confidential decision and medical information stays with the appropriate process. Avoid using a broad team email as the decision letter or copying private reasons merely to make the arrangement seem acceptable.

check.question: A requested tool is denied and another option is offered. What does the state policy require the decision explanation to address?
check.correct: Why the requested option is denied and why the offered accommodation will be effective, with the required plain-language written explanation.
wrong: Only that the offered tool is cheaper.
A statement that every supervisor may deny a request without consultation.
An instruction not to seek any review of the decision.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. The explanation needs both sides of the decision, not a generic label. The coordinator’s required involvement and the agency’s review process still apply.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A cheaper product does not by itself explain why an offered alternative will be effective. Supervisor involvement does not remove the required ADA Coordinator consultation before denial. The agency must also provide its designated review process, so an instruction never to seek review is not the policy approach. Use the authorized plain-language written explanation with specific reasons and appropriate next steps.

sorting.heading: Which kind of message is this?

items.text: We have identified two options and still need to check effectiveness.
The approved tool will be configured by the assigned support contact.
The written denial must explain the specific reasons and the review route.
The employee has described a barrier in the proposed alternative.
The recurring meeting arrangement is ready for the next scheduled meeting.
The alternative decision must explain why it will be effective.

lessons.next: The final lesson follows the decision into real work and considers when to reopen the conversation.

scenario.context: In this example, a manager drafts a denial saying only “not feasible” and wants to send it without ADA Coordinator consultation.
options: Send it immediately because short explanations are always clearer.
Consult the coordinator as required and use the authorized process for a specific plain-language written explanation and review information.
Explain the employee’s diagnosis to the entire team first.
responses: A short label does not provide the required specific explanation or consultation. Clarity does not mean removing the reasons a person needs.
This follows the policy and keeps the decision understandable. Do not assume the outcome before the required review.
Medical disclosure is unrelated to explaining an authorized decision to the requester and would compromise confidentiality.

lessons.transfer: Draft an implementation update for a practice approved adjustment. State what is approved, what is pending, who is responsible and when the next update is expected.

move.control: You can help make the communication clear while respecting decision authority.
move.failure: An informal preference or vague label becomes an unsupported final decision.
move.next: Verify the responsible process and check that the person receives a clear result and appropriate next steps.

lessons.title: Check effectiveness and return when conditions change
lessons.summary: The conversation remains useful when an adjustment is delayed, fails or no longer fits the task.
lessons.objective: Distinguish approved, implemented and effective accommodation.
objectives: Distinguish approved, implemented and effective accommodation.
Plan a focused follow-up that does not request unnecessary new medical information.
Identify a changed circumstance that should return to the appropriate process.
takeaways: An approval is not proof that the adjustment is available or effective.
Status communication and feasible temporary measures matter during delay.
Changed tasks or conditions may require another exchange through the process.
lessons.statement: A decision becomes useful when it works in the person’s actual employment situation and stays responsive to change.

image.caption: Follow-up gives people a way to say whether a change works without starting a new medical interview.

intro.heading: Close the action, not the relationship
intro.body:
The practice analyst’s tool is approved and installed, but it does not work with the agency’s actual report template. The supervisor has a purchase receipt and wants to close the request. That would confuse installation with effectiveness. Ask about the task result and bring the remaining barrier to the appropriate staff. A genuine check can be brief: whether the person can complete the required activity and what still needs attention.

During delay, MMB Policy 1433 calls for prompt provision of an approved accommodation and status communication in the circumstances described by the policy. If an approved accommodation cannot be provided within a reasonable time, the decision maker informs the requester before the end of 30 days. Where feasible, temporary measures provide assistance. This is not a universal permission to wait 30 days or a promise that every request finishes within that period. Keep the status and responsibility accurate.

After an adjustment works, changed circumstances may require a new conversation. A new system, duty, meeting format or condition can affect effectiveness. An employee’s earlier success does not prove that the old arrangement remains suitable forever. Respond to the changed barrier and involve the coordinator about any appropriate documentation; do not request medical proof yourself or repeatedly reopen a settled medical question without a proper reason.

Keep the authorized records and confidentiality boundaries. A team can improve its process using non-identifying lessons about delay or recurring barriers, but should not turn the review into a list of diagnoses, personal IDI results or coworkers’ accommodation histories. Good follow-up preserves both the work purpose and the person’s dignity. It gives the employee a clear contact and gives the supervisor an honest understanding of what has actually been implemented.

inThisLesson: Revisit changed barriers through the process.
lessons.keyStatement: A completed purchase or closed note is not the same as an effective accommodation.

flashcards.back: The authorized process has decided to provide an adjustment. Practical implementation may still be pending.
The arrangement or tool has been provided. Its usefulness in the task still needs attention.
The adjustment addresses the relevant barrier and supports the employment purpose in the actual circumstances.
A further conversation through the appropriate process when a changed need or unresolved barrier requires attention.

items.title: Ask about the result
items.body: Ask whether the adjustment supports the intended task or employment benefit, and listen to specific remaining barriers. Installation can be complete while effectiveness remains unresolved. Describe that distinction without judging gratitude or collecting medical material. The person’s experience and relevant task checks help the responsible process identify what needs attention next.

items.title: Respond to delay
items.body: Identify the pending step, responsible contact and next update. Policy 1433 calls for prompt provision and, in its specified approved-but-delayed circumstances, a status update before the end of 30 days; it also calls for feasible temporary assistance during delay. The condition is not a general waiting period or a guaranteed completion date. Keep communication and the current task need visible while the longer step proceeds.

items.title: Plan for change
items.body: Give the employee a clear way to raise a barrier when the task or arrangement changes. Revisit effectiveness with appropriate guidance rather than treating an old approval as a permanent guarantee. A new conversation can address changed software or duties without asking for a complete medical file from the supervisor. Preserve confidentiality and actual decision responsibilities as the work evolves.

tabs.label: A decision email
tabs.body: A decision email can establish approval, but delivery and effectiveness are additional questions. Confirm what was actually arranged and whether the intended task is supported. If implementation is delayed, communicate the current step and appropriate next contact. Treating the email as completion can leave the employee with the same barrier even though the formal decision was favorable.

tabs.label: A purchase receipt
tabs.body: A receipt shows that something was purchased. It does not show correct installation, configuration or access to the required fields. Ask which setup and task checks remain and who will complete them through the responsible process. Money spent is useful implementation evidence, not a reason to dismiss a report that the adjustment remains ineffective or demand gratitude for an unresolved barrier.

tabs.label: A task conversation
tabs.body: A task conversation can identify what works and what still fails in the employee’s experience. Combine it with relevant specialist checks and the appropriate process when needed, without treating it as a medical interrogation. If a new barrier appears after an update, identify the changed task conditions. The next response should address current effectiveness rather than assume that an earlier approval or purchase permanently settled every need.

check.question: A purchased tool is installed but still cannot support the employee’s required task. What should the follow-up say?
check.correct: The tool has been installed, but effectiveness remains unresolved and needs attention through the accommodation process.
wrong: The request is complete because money was spent.
The employee must be ungrateful if they report a remaining barrier.
A new complete medical file must be sent to the supervisor immediately.
check.feedbackCorrect: Yes. This separates implementation from effectiveness and provides the proper next route. The remaining barrier deserves inquiry rather than an assumption about the person.
check.feedbackIncorrect: A purchase does not prove that the accommodation works. Avoid judgments about gratitude and improper documentation requests; focus on the task and responsible process.

items.text: The authorized decision says the adjustment will be provided.
The tool is installed on the employee’s actual workstation.
Can the employee now review every required field?
The coordinator communicates approval of the recurring arrangement.
The agreed meeting support is present at the next meeting.
Does the support allow effective participation in this meeting format?

lessons.next: Use the job aid to prepare a respectful exchange and follow it through. The related supervisor and accessibility courses address the wider responsibilities around the conversation.

scenario.context: In this example, an employee’s accommodation worked until a software update changed the task. The supervisor says the old approval means no further conversation is needed.
options: Recognize the changed barrier, discuss the work result and involve the appropriate process to consider an effective response.
Close the conversation because the original request was approved.
Share the employee’s medical history to explain why the software update is a problem.
responses: This uses the process responsively and keeps the focus on current effectiveness. Any documentation question belongs with the coordinator.
An old approval does not establish current effectiveness after conditions change.
The team needs the relevant work facts, not a medical history. Preserve confidentiality while coordinating a response.

lessons.transfer: Write a practice follow-up using three separate statements: what was approved, what is now available and what remains to be checked.

move.control: You can check the actual task and return to the process when conditions change.
move.failure: A receipt or old approval is treated as proof of lasting effectiveness.
move.next: Confirm the current work result and give the person a clear contact for any remaining barrier.

jobAid.subtitle: Prepare and follow through on an accommodation exchange
remember: The employee’s participation and preferences matter.
The supervisor describes work; the coordinator handles appropriate medical documentation.
A customary method is not automatically an essential function.
Formal decisions and confidential records stay in the authorized agency process.

sections.heading: Prepare the exchange
items: Explain the purpose, roles and accessible participation arrangements.
Respect requested support-person participation through the process.
Identify the work duty, barrier and outcome without collecting a medical history.

sections.heading: Consider the options
items: Summarize what you heard and invite correction.
Compare the actual effectiveness of options, seriously considering the person’s preference.
Name uncertainty and route hardship, threat, documentation or denial questions to the appropriate authority.

sections.heading: Explain and check
items: Distinguish discussion, authorized decision and implementation.
Use required consultation and specific written explanations for denial and offered alternatives.
Communicate delay, check effectiveness and revisit changed circumstances while preserving confidentiality.
